nodes.question: What is meant by 'creative destruction' in the context of the paragraph?
nodes.answer: 'Creative destruction' refers to the idea that some indirect impacts of disasters could be positive, often associated with rebuilding efforts that improve or innovate upon previous conditions.
nodes.paragraph: There appears to be only weak evidence of whether of the losses they cause exceed those arising from the direct impact of the events and may depend on what one defines as indirect impacts (Botzen et al. 2019 ; Sousa et al. 2022 ). Finally, these indirect impacts could also plausibly be positive, i.e, what is often called creative destruction or build back better in the literature (Hallegatte et al. 2018 ). Given the complexity of explicitly modeling the indirect impacts of natural disasters directly, most studies limit themselves to using some measures of the direct damages or a proxy driving the direct damages to capture both the direct and indirect impacts (Botzen et al. 2019 ).4 Again, a graphical illustration is helpful; see Fig. 1. Accordingly, the two basic inputs are the physical characteristics of the event and the physical characteristics of the location, where these may both be multi-dimensional. These two vectors of inputs will then feed into a damage function that translates the event to the subsequent direct damage. 4 The few studies that have explicitly measured the indirect impacts do so generally at a regional or national level using Input-Output tables or Computer General Equilibrium models (Botzen et al.

nodes.question: What plan is a fundamental driving force behind the initiatives mentioned in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan (RTRP) presented by the Spanish Government in October 2020 is a fundamental driving force.
nodes.paragraph: Also, the NECP envisages the need for higher taxes on heavily polluting activities. The Technical Building Code laysdown new building regulations, to ensure that domestic energy consumption is low. A fundamental driving force behind many of these initiatives will be the Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan (RTRP), presented by the Spanish Government inOctober 2020, which proposes assigning 39% of the funds that Spain receives under the Next Generation EU (NGEU) programme to the green transition; see Cansino et al. (2016) for a description of the policy measures to control carbon emissions in Spain. Ensuring that energy policies are as effective as possible requires an understanding of the main dynamics and drivers of emissions. Within this context, the interest in modelling and forecasting GHG emissions is without doubt. Carbon dioxide (CO 2) emissions, largely by-products of energy consumption, account for the largest share of GHG and, consequently, the analysis of GHG emissions has usually focused on CO 2 emissions; see, for instance, Friedlingstein et al. ( 2022 ), who describes the Global Carbon Project that produces world-wide projections of CO 2emissions in preparing the annual Global Carbon Budget, which is considered in the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPPC) reports.
